statement: In a series of coroners' cases from Victoria, Australia (Pilgrim et al., 2011), MDMA was measured in postmortem blood above 0.02 mg/L in 106 of 14,682 deaths with full toxicology testing between 2002 and 2008 (78 in 100 men; ages 17 to 48, median 25; 60 in 100 by external injury such as hanging or a vehicle crash). Of the 106, 20 had MDMA alone or with MDA, 34 had MDMA with alcohol, 33 had other drugs judged unlikely to cause a drug reaction, and 19 had a combination that the authors rated as a risk of harmful interaction (4 major, all with moclobemide, an antidepressant of the MAO-inhibitor type; 10 moderate; 5 minor). The 19 are a subset chosen by the authors for such combinations, so the counts below describe them and not all deaths involving MDMA. Among the 19, by editors' tally, blood held methamphetamine or amphetamine in 15, antidepressants in 13 (moclobemide in 4, others in 9), opioids in 12 (methadone, codeine and morphine in 5 each, tramadol in 1, and 6-MAM, a marker of heroin, in 3, so some opioids may not have been medicines), benzodiazepines in 8, paracetamol or ibuprofen in 4, cannabis in 5 and alcohol in 3; a benzodiazepine or an opioid was present in 14. Doctors or paramedics noted signs of serotonin toxicity before death in 3 of the 4 moclobemide cases (postmortem blood MDMA 1.0 to 2.6 mg/L); in other cases the authors think it more likely that it was overlooked or could not be diagnosed, which the data cannot show. Drug toxicity alone was recorded as the cause of death in 12 of the 19, injury plus drug toxicity in 2, and other causes (drowning, train impact, blood loss, hanging, carbon monoxide) in 5. Where the medicines came from was mostly unknown; in two moclobemide cases witnesses suggested a friend or family member. A narrative review reports, second-hand, 75 UK deaths attributed to ecstasy in 1997 to 2000 in which other drugs, mainly opiates and sedatives, were also found in 93 in 100 (Schifano et al., as summarized by Parrott, 2004). The limits are that a blood test after death cannot show who took what, when, how much or why, concentrations can change after death and are not doses, the series is one Australian state, and the risk groups follow a drug-information database and the authors' judgment.
plain: In one Australian study of 106 deaths with MDMA in the blood (2002 to 2008), 19 (about 18 in 100) also had a combination of drugs that the authors rated as risky. MDMA in the blood does not by itself show that MDMA caused a death: 6 in 10 of the 106 died of injuries such as hanging or a crash. Among those 19, 15 also had methamphetamine or amphetamine, 13 an antidepressant, 12 an opioid and 8 a benzodiazepine. Four had moclobemide, an antidepressant of the MAO-inhibitor type, and three of those four showed signs of serotonin toxicity before they died. These 19 were picked for risky mixes, so the numbers do not show how common any mix is in deaths with MDMA. A blood test after death cannot show who took what, when or why, and where the medicines came from was mostly unknown. A second-hand report of 75 UK deaths found other drugs, mostly opiates and sedatives, in 93 in 100.
population: People who died in Victoria, Australia, in 2002 to 2008 with MDMA above 0.02 mg/L in postmortem blood (106 of 14,682 coroners' cases with full toxicology; 78% male, median age 25, 60% death by external injury), of whom 19 (14 men, ages 21 to 45) were examined in detail; plus 75 UK deaths attributed to ecstasy in 1997 to 2000, second-hand
exposure: MDMA found in blood together with other drugs or medicines, grouped by the authors' rating of interaction risk (major: moclobemide; moderate: dothiepin, amphetamines, tramadol, venlafaxine, cocaine, methadone, fluoxetine; minor: doxylamine and some SSRIs)
comparator: The other 87 cases in the series (MDMA alone or with MDA, with alcohol, or with drugs unlikely to cause a reaction); no comparison with deaths without MDMA or with living people who took MDMA
outcome: Which other drugs and medicines were found in postmortem blood in the 19 cases, and the recorded cause of death
magnitude: Series: 106 deaths with blood MDMA above 0.02 mg/L among 14,682 coroners' cases with full toxicology, 2002-2008; 83 (78%) men, ages 17-48 (median 25), 64 (60%) external injury. Of the 106: MDMA alone or with MDA 20 (about 19 in 100, editors' arithmetic), with ethanol 34 (32), with other drugs unlikely to cause a reaction 33 (31), examined in detail 19 (18). The 19 (14 men, ages 21-45, median 28): group 1 major 4 (all moclobemide; MDMA 1.0-2.6 mg/L, median 1.85; serotonin toxicity signs noted before death in 3), group 2 moderate 10 (MDMA 0.02-3.5, median 0.07), group 3 minor 5 (MDMA 0.2-1.4, median 0.2). Editors' tally of Table II, cases with at least one substance: methamphetamine or amphetamine 15; antidepressant 13 (moclobemide 4, other 9); opioid 12 (11 without 6-MAM); benzodiazepine or metabolite 8; benzodiazepine or opioid 14; paracetamol or ibuprofen 4; cannabis 5; ethanol 3. Cause of death: drug toxicity alone 12, injury plus drug toxicity 2, other 5. Second-hand (Parrott, 2004, Table 3): 75 UK deaths attributed to ecstasy 1997-2000, other drugs also in 93% of cases, mainly opiates and sedatives. No intervals; the 19 are an author-selected subset, so no rate of any combination can be derived.

evidence.locator: Methods, Toxicological analysis (1st and 2nd paragraphs), Cohort selection, Data analysis, and Table I (p. 220)
evidence.extracted: Cases came from the Australian National Coroners Information System: all closed Victorian cases between January 2002 and December 2008 with a positive, quantified MDMA result above 0.02 mg/L in postmortem blood (femoral vein blood where possible, to limit redistribution). Toxicology used immunoassay screening and confirmation by gas chromatography with mass spectrometry, with a lower limit of quantitation for MDMA of 0.02 mg/L. The authors assessed each case's other drugs and the likelihood of a toxic reaction, including the risk of serotonin toxicity. Table I groups the drugs found: major interaction, moclobemide (a reversible MAO-A inhibitor; hypertensive crisis and serotonin toxicity); moderate interaction, dothiepin (a tricyclic antidepressant), amphetamine and derivatives (amphetamine, methamphetamine, MDA, MDEA), tramadol, venlafaxine and cocaine (serotonin toxicity), and methadone and fluoxetine (CYP2D6 inhibitors, raising MDMA concentrations); minor interaction, doxylamine and the SSRIs citalopram, sertraline and fluvoxamine.

evidence.locator: Methods, Data analysis, the paragraphs beginning 'Cases demonstrating a risk of ST' and ''Major' interactions were those' (p. 223); Results, Basic characteristics, 1st to 3rd paragraphs (p. 223)
evidence.extracted: Cases showing a risk of serotonin toxicity or another adverse drug reaction were examined more closely, and other cases (MDMA alone, or with drugs unlikely to produce a reaction) were excluded from further investigation because the cohort focused on toxic drug combinations only. Cases were grouped as major, moderate or minor interaction by risk of drug toxicity from a drug-information database and other references; fluoxetine and paroxetine were counted as moderate because their strong inhibition of the enzyme CYP2D6 can raise MDMA concentrations, and the weak inhibition by sertraline and citalopram was taken as unlikely to contribute to a fatal reaction. Results: 106 cases between 2002 and 2008 with quantified MDMA above the minimum level, among 14,682 coroners' cases that had full toxicological testing; 83 (78%) were male and 64 (60%) died by external injury (for example hangings, motor vehicle crashes); ages 17 to 48, median 25. Of the 106, 4 were a major risk, 10 moderate and 5 minor (Table II); these 19 were examined in detail. The other 87 were MDMA alone or with MDA as metabolite (20), MDMA with ethanol (34) or MDMA with other drugs not likely to cause an adverse drug reaction (33).
evidence.quote: this cohort focused on toxic drug combinations only

evidence.locator: Table II, the 19 cases (pp. 221-223): columns Cause of Death and Autopsy Findings and Postmortem Blood Drug Concentration
evidence.extracted: Table II lists each of the 19 cases by group with sex and age, cause of death and autopsy findings, the drugs found in postmortem blood with concentrations, and the specimen site and postmortem interval. Group 1 (cases 1 to 4): all four had moclobemide. Groups 2 (cases 5 to 14) and 3 (cases 15 to 19) held, besides the drugs that defined the group, combinations of methamphetamine, amphetamine, opioids (codeine, morphine, methadone, tramadol, 6-MAM), benzodiazepines and their metabolites (diazepam, alprazolam, temazepam, oxazepam, nordiazepam, 7-aminoflunitrazepam), other antidepressants (dothiepin, venlafaxine, fluoxetine, sertraline, citalopram, fluvoxamine, mirtazapine), paracetamol, ibuprofen, cannabis (THC) and ethanol, and in single cases ketamine, p-methoxyamphetamine, olanzapine, metoclopramide and frusemide. Editors' tally of the table's rows, cases with at least one: methamphetamine or amphetamine 15 (methamphetamine 14, amphetamine 7); antidepressant 13 (moclobemide 4, others 9); opioid 12 (11 without 6-MAM; methadone 5, codeine 5, morphine 5, tramadol 1, 6-MAM 3); benzodiazepine or metabolite 8 (cases 5, 6, 8, 9, 10, 14, 15, 19); benzodiazepine or opioid 14; paracetamol or ibuprofen 4; cannabis 5; ethanol 3; blood MDMA 0.05 mg/L or less in 5 cases (6, 8, 9, 13, 14). Cause of death: drug toxicity alone in 12 (cases 1-5, 7, 9, 10, 12, 15, 18, 19), injury plus combined drug toxicity in 2 (13, 17), and drowning, train impact, hemorrhagic shock, hanging or carbon monoxide poisoning in the other 5.

evidence.locator: Results, Toxicology findings in the 19 cases of interest, 1st paragraph (begins p. 223, ends p. 224), 2nd and 3rd paragraphs (p. 224)
evidence.extracted: The 19 cases were mostly male (14), aged 21 to 45 (median 28). The four Group 1 cases all involved moclobemide, with postmortem blood MDMA 1.0 to 2.6 mg/L (median 1.85); clinical symptoms of serotonin toxicity were reported by a paramedic or physician in three of them (cases 1 to 3). Group 2 (10 cases) had fluoxetine, venlafaxine, methadone, dothiepin and tramadol with MDMA, and also paramethoxyamphetamine and methamphetamine, with MDMA 0.02 to 3.5 mg/L (median 0.07). Group 3 (5 cases) involved citalopram, fluvoxamine, sertraline and/or doxylamine, with MDMA 0.2 to 1.4 mg/L (median 0.2).

evidence.locator: Discussion, 1st paragraph and the paragraph beginning 'In this cohort, ST was reported'
evidence.extracted: Four cases involved moclobemide with MDMA, a combination associated with serotonin toxicity; the authors note that moclobemide was originally marketed as a safer alternative to older MAO inhibitors and that a search across Australia would probably find more such deaths. Serotonin toxicity was reported from symptoms witnessed before death in three cases (1 to 3); despite the possibility in many other cases, including moderate-risk cases with serotonin-active drugs, it was not reported. The authors consider it more likely that it was overlooked, or that the lack of symptoms before death (for example when the person was found dead) prevented a diagnosis, than that it did not occur.

evidence.locator: Discussion, the paragraph beginning 'In the Copeland et al. study' (begins p. 224, ends p. 225); Limitations paragraph; Conclusions, 1st paragraph (p. 225)
evidence.extracted: In many postmortem cases the source of the drugs, licit or illicit, remains unknown unless a medicolegal investigation specifies it, which was unusual here; witness statements in a number of cases, including two of the moclobemide cases with fatal serotonin toxicity, suggested that the person may have obtained the medicines from a friend or family member. Limitations the authors state: postmortem redistribution may alter drug concentrations (some specimens were taken days after death, for example six days in case 18, or from non-peripheral sites such as cavity blood in case 10); missing information, including the source of the drugs (prescribing information) and clinical data such as temperature; people are usually found dead, so symptoms go unreported; and concentrations of drugs that produce tolerance, such as morphine, are hard to interpret. Conclusions: some people who use ecstasy may combine pharmaceutical drugs to strengthen the effect or ease the comedown, but this appeared to be a limited practice in Victoria in 2002-2008; people taking medicines for treatment who occasionally use ecstasy are at risk, particularly if unaware of interactions; many of the deaths were apparently unintentional drug toxicity, so knowledge of these interactions is likely to be limited.

Parrott's Table 3, as summarized: Schifano et al. (2003), UK 1997-2000, toxicological analyses of 75 deaths attributed to ecstasy, XTC, MDMA or MDA: 91% MDMA, 9% MDA, other drugs also found in 93% of cases, mainly opiates and sedatives.

risk_of_bias.note: A case series: the 19 were selected by the authors for drug combinations they rated as risky, and the medicines were found in postmortem blood, which cannot show who took what or when; no comparison group.

inconsistency.note: Not rated: one series and one second-hand row that point the same way.

indirectness.note: The question is what else is found in deaths involving MDMA; the series answers it only for a selected subset of 106 deaths in one state, and the second series comes second-hand.

imprecision.note: 19 cases, no intervals, no denominators for any combination.

grade.reasoning: A descriptive case series starts low (METHODS 6.3); risk of bias, indirectness and imprecision each take a level, and the result is very low. Status single-study: one primary series, with a second-hand row from a narrative review that points the same way. Stays at draft because it rests on a case series and a narrative review (brief; METHODS 6.3, 12). The claim describes what was found together in a selected set of deaths, not how common any mix is, and gives no advice.

verification.flag_note: Rests on one case series (Pilgrim et al., 2011) and one second-hand row from Parrott (2004). Stays at draft as the brief asks for case reports. Related ground is covered by the claim on voluntary reports of ecstasy with prescribed medicines (cl_mdma_medicine_reports, Reader 51), which the editor may join with this one. The abstract of the paper says 43 (41%) cases involved other drugs, but its Results give 19 + 33 = 52; the text counts four cases with pulmonary oedema against five in Table II and names chlorpromazine and chlorpheniramine, which no table lists; 'opioids' include 6-MAM (a heroin marker) in 3 cases and morphine and codeine that may come from heroin or from medicines. Schifano et al. (2003, BMJ), Silins et al. (2007; a reference record exists), Copeland et al. (2006) and Cohen et al. (2021) were not read here.
